stage: HISTORIE (engine stage 6) - fractal axis + competing frames - cache
disputedNote: Even where this story begins is disputed - picking a start date is itself a position. Frames change emphasis and annotation, never the record.

frames.label: Jun 2026 resignation
frames.note: The story begins this week, when John Healey and his deputy walked out over the size of Starmer's defence package. Read this way, it is a Westminster authority crisis about a Labour PM losing his defence secretary days before a NATO summit. This is the frame Conservative critics like Kemi Badenoch and Healey's allies open with.

frames.label: Feb 2022 Ukraine invasion
frames.note: The story begins with Russia's full invasion of Ukraine, after which NATO's 2% floor was widely treated as a ceiling that no longer matched the threat. Read this way, Healey's exit is the moment a post-2022 spending trajectory finally collided with a Treasury that would not fund it. This is the frame defence-establishment voices and the France 24 'Putin will be watching' commentary open with.

frames.label: 2010 SDSR cuts
frames.note: The story begins with the 2010 Strategic Defence and Security Review and the austerity-era contraction of the armed forces. Read this way, the current row is one more episode in a 15-year argument about whether any UK government will pay for the military it claims to want. This is the frame long-view defence analysts and Treasury-history commentators open with.

bands.label: Resignation and Jarvis handover
bands.summary: Healey and his number two quit over Starmer's defence settlement, Dan Jarvis is appointed, and cabinet ministers are asked to find cuts to fund a larger military uplift before the NATO summit.

nodes.title: Healey and his deputy resign over defence settlement
nodes.what: Defence Secretary John Healey and his number two quit the government after talks with No 10 and the Treasury over the size of the next defence package. They said the settlement on offer would not give the armed forces what they had been promised, and walked out days before the NATO summit.
nodes.disputed: Healey's allies describe the exit as a principled stand that the proposed uplift was too small to match the threat; Downing Street describes it as a disagreement over pace within a settlement that still raises defence spending.

nodes.title: Dan Jarvis appointed defence secretary
nodes.what: Keir Starmer moved Dan Jarvis, the Makerfield MP and former Army officer, into the Ministry of Defence within hours of the resignations. Jarvis said he had a 'big responsibility' to secure the funds the armed forces needed and would push inside government for the package Healey had argued for.

nodes.title: Cabinet told to find cuts to fund defence uplift
nodes.what: Starmer and Rachel Reeves asked cabinet ministers to identify spending reductions in their own departments to pay for a larger military settlement. Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy publicly confirmed Whitehall departments were being asked to absorb cuts so the headline defence figure could rise before the NATO summit.
nodes.disputed: Treasury-aligned ministers describe the exercise as a normal trade-off inside a tight fiscal envelope; Healey's supporters and Conservative critics describe it as evidence the original defence offer was inadequate and is only being topped up under pressure.

nodes.title: UK forces board sanctioned Russian tanker in the Channel
nodes.what: Royal Marines and Army personnel boarded the sanctioned Russian-linked oil tanker Smyrtos in the English Channel, the first such action by UK forces against a vessel described as part of the 'shadow fleet.' Starmer announced the boarding the same day he was defending his defence plan against the Healey-led revolt.

nodes.title: Starmer to publish defence investment plan before NATO summit
nodes.what: Starmer said the government would publish its defence investment plan ahead of the NATO summit later in the month, setting out the spending trajectory and capability commitments the UK would take into the alliance meeting. Kemi Badenoch challenged Starmer to match higher allied targets, while Jarvis said Labour had to 'meet the moment' on defence.

bands.label: Labour in office, defence under review
bands.summary: Starmer's Labour government takes power, commissions a defence review, and negotiates internally over how fast to raise military spending against welfare and net-zero priorities.

nodes.title: Starmer takes office, Healey appointed defence secretary
nodes.what: After Labour's general election win, Keir Starmer formed a government and named John Healey, the party's long-serving shadow defence spokesman, as Secretary of State for Defence. Luke Pollard was appointed Minister for the Armed Forces. The new team inherited a Ministry of Defence equipment programme widely described in official reports as unaffordable.

nodes.title: Strategic Defence Review commissioned
nodes.what: Healey announced a Strategic Defence Review led by former NATO Secretary General George Robertson, alongside Fiona Hill and General Sir Richard Barrons, with a remit to report within a year. The review was framed as the first since 2021 and the basis for moving toward a 2.5 percent of GDP spending floor 'when fiscal conditions allow'. The MoD said it would consider threats, capabilities and force structure together.

nodes.title: Starmer pledges 2.5 percent by 2027, funded by aid cuts
nodes.what: Days before a Washington visit, Starmer told the Commons UK defence spending would rise to 2.5 percent of GDP from April 2027, with an ambition of 3 percent in the next parliament. The increase was to be paid for by cutting the overseas development assistance budget from 0.5 to 0.3 percent of gross national income. International Development Minister Anneliese Dodds resigned in protest the following week.
nodes.disputed: Downing Street described the package as the largest sustained defence increase since the Cold War; aid-sector and some Labour MPs described it as funding rearmament by cutting the world's poorest, with the trade-off itself contested as a political choice rather than a fiscal necessity.

nodes.title: Strategic Defence Review published
nodes.what: The Robertson-led review was published, recommending a shift to 'warfighting readiness', investment in nuclear, drones, cyber and munitions stockpiles, and a larger reserve force. The government accepted all 62 recommendations in principle but linked the full programme to a future 3 percent of GDP path that was not yet funded. Service chiefs publicly welcomed the document while flagging that capability choices depended on the next spending review.

nodes.title: NATO Hague summit raises the spending bar
nodes.what: At the NATO summit in The Hague, allies agreed a new headline target of 5 percent of GDP on defence and security, split between 3.5 percent of core military spending and 1.5 percent on wider resilience, to be reached by 2035. Starmer signed the communique, committing the UK to a trajectory well beyond the 2.5 percent already announced. The summit declaration left each ally to set its own glide path.

nodes.title: Spring statement signals tighter defence settlement
nodes.what: Chancellor Rachel Reeves used the spring fiscal statement to confirm that the 2.5 percent target would be hit on schedule but pushed any movement toward the NATO 3.5 percent core figure into the next parliament. Treasury briefings stressed that further increases would require trade-offs against welfare, the NHS and net zero. Healey and Pollard pressed inside cabinet for a faster ramp tied to the SDR's capability assumptions.
nodes.disputed: Treasury officials presented the settlement as the maximum compatible with the fiscal rules; defence ministers and service chiefs described it as a gap between the SDR force the government had endorsed and the budget it was willing to fund.

nodes.title: Pre-summit cabinet row over defence package
nodes.what: In the run-up to the 2026 NATO summit, Starmer convened cabinet to agree a defence settlement that would brief credibly to allies. Reports described Healey and Pollard arguing for a larger uplift, with other cabinet ministers asked to find departmental savings to part-fund it. The dispute over the size and pace of the increase set the stage for the resignations that followed.

bands.label: Ukraine war reshapes NATO pressure
bands.summary: Russia's invasion of Ukraine pushes UK and allied defence-spending expectations well above the old 2% NATO floor and reframes the political baseline Healey inherits.

nodes.title: Russia launches full-scale invasion of Ukraine
nodes.what: Russian forces crossed into Ukraine from the north, east and south, beginning the largest land war in Europe since 1945. NATO members rapidly moved to reinforce the eastern flank and began funnelling weapons and training to Kyiv. The invasion reset assumptions across European capitals about the scale and immediacy of conventional military threat.

nodes.title: UK pledges sustained military aid to Ukraine
nodes.what: The Johnson government announced expanded supplies of anti-tank weapons, air defence systems and training, building on shipments begun before the invasion. Ministers framed the package as open-ended, tying UK defence planning to a long Ukrainian war. The commitments became a recurring pressure point on the Ministry of Defence budget through 2022 and 2023.

nodes.title: NATO Madrid summit adopts new Strategic Concept
nodes.what: Allied leaders meeting in Madrid named Russia the most significant and direct threat to allied security and approved a new force model with higher readiness levels. The summit also invited Finland and Sweden to join the alliance. Defence ministries across NATO began planning for larger standing commitments than the post-Cold-War norm.

nodes.title: Sunak government publishes Integrated Review Refresh
nodes.what: The refreshed UK Integrated Review described Russia as the most acute threat to European security and set an aspiration to raise defence spending to 2.5% of GDP when fiscal conditions allowed. The document also committed extra money to the nuclear enterprise and munitions stockpiles. It left the timing of the 2.5% target deliberately conditional, a point opposition and service chiefs returned to repeatedly.

nodes.title: NATO Vilnius summit hardens 2% as a floor
nodes.what: At Vilnius allied leaders agreed that 2% of GDP on defence should be treated as a minimum rather than a target, with several members already spending well above it. The summit also produced new defence plans for the alliance's regions and a multi-year package for Ukraine. The shift from ceiling to floor reframed what counted as a credible UK commitment.

nodes.title: Labour wins general election with defence-review pledge
nodes.what: Keir Starmer's Labour party won a large Commons majority on a manifesto that promised a Strategic Defence Review and a path to 2.5% of GDP without naming a year. John Healey, shadow defence secretary since 2020, was appointed Secretary of State for Defence the following day. The new government inherited the Ukraine aid commitments, the Vilnius floor and an undated 2.5% aspiration.

bands.label: Post-SDSR austerity era for the MoD
bands.summary: From the 2010 Strategic Defence and Security Review onward, successive UK governments cut force structure and held defence spending near the NATO minimum, leaving the capability gap that later spending fights are trying to close.

nodes.title: Cameron coalition publishes the 2010 Strategic Defence and Security Review
nodes.what: The new Conservative-Liberal Democrat government released the SDSR alongside the spending review, cutting around 8 percent from the defence budget over four years. The review scrapped the Nimrod MRA4 maritime patrol aircraft, retired HMS Ark Royal and the Harrier fleet early, and reduced Army, Navy and RAF personnel numbers. Carrier strike capability was placed in a planned gap until the new Queen Elizabeth class entered service.
nodes.disputed: The Ministry of Defence described the review as a necessary correction to an overheated equipment plan inherited from Labour; senior former service chiefs and defence commentators described it as a Treasury-driven contraction that opened capability gaps the UK would spend a decade trying to close.

nodes.title: NATO Wales Summit formalises the 2 percent of GDP defence spending pledge
nodes.what: At the Newport summit hosted by David Cameron months after Russia annexed Crimea, NATO heads of state and government endorsed the Defence Investment Pledge. Allies below the 2 percent of GDP threshold committed to move toward it within a decade, and to spend at least 20 percent of defence budgets on major equipment. The pledge became the benchmark every subsequent UK government measured itself against.

nodes.title: SDSR 2015 commits to keep UK defence spending at 2 percent of GDP
nodes.what: Cameron's majority Conservative government published a second SDSR that reversed some of the 2010 personnel reductions and pledged to meet the NATO 2 percent floor every year of the decade. It funded two new strike brigades, additional F-35 orders, nine P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft to fill the post-Nimrod gap, and confirmed the Successor nuclear deterrent. Critics noted the accounting changes that helped the headline figure reach 2 percent.

nodes.title: Johnson government publishes the Integrated Review, 'Global Britain in a Competitive Age'
nodes.what: The review set out an Indo-Pacific tilt, named Russia as the most acute threat and China as a systemic competitor, and announced an increase in the nuclear warhead cap. It was paired with a four-year, 24 billion pound cash uplift for defence announced the previous November, the largest such commitment since the end of the Cold War in nominal terms.

nodes.title: Defence Command Paper cuts the Army to 72,500 and retires older platforms
nodes.what: Defence Secretary Ben Wallace presented 'Defence in a Competitive Age', reducing the regular Army from a target of 82,000 to 72,500 by 2025 and retiring tranche 1 Typhoons, C-130 Hercules and older Warrior and Challenger 2 numbers. Wallace framed the changes as a shift toward cyber, space and modernised heavy armour; opposition spokesperson John Healey called the headcount cut a broken manifesto promise.

cites.l: GOV.UK: Defence in a Competitive Age

nodes.disputed: The Ministry of Defence presented the changes as modernisation that traded mass for technology; Labour, the Defence Select Committee and former chiefs of the general staff described them as a further hollowing-out of the Army at a moment of rising threat.
